claim: Ixodes scapularis ticks have an adiponectin receptor-like protein (ISARL).
source: In this study, we demonstrate that Ixodes scapularis ticks have an adiponectin receptor-like protein (ISARL) but lack adiponectin, suggesting activation by alternative pathways.
evidence: The manuscript describes identification and characterization of ISARL through database searches and sequence analysis.

claim: Ixodes scapularis ticks lack adiponectin.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that Ixodes scapularis ticks have an adiponectin receptor-like protein (ISARL) but lack adiponectin, suggesting activation by alternative pathways.
evidence: The manuscript reports that no tick genes with high homology to human and mouse adiponectin were found in database searches.

claim: ISARL expression is significantly upregulated in the tick gut after Borrelia burgdorferi infection.
source: ISARL expression is significantly upregulated in the tick gut after Borrelia burgdorferi infection, suggesting that ISARL signaling may be co-opted by the Lyme disease agent.
evidence: Figure 1A shows qPCR data demonstrating significantly increased ISARL expression (p<0.0001) in nymphal tick guts after feeding on B. burgdorferi-infected mice.

claim: RNAi-mediated silencing of ISARL significantly reduced the B. burgdorferi burden in the tick.
source: Consistent with this, RNA interference (RNAi)-mediated silencing of ISARL significantly reduced the B. burgdorferi burden in the tick.
evidence: Figure 1D shows qPCR data demonstrating marked reduction (p<0.001) of B. burgdorferi burden in ISARL-silenced nymph guts.

claim: ISARL-mediated phospholipid metabolism by phosphatidylserine synthase I is associated with B. burgdorferi survival.
source: RNA-seq-based transcriptomics and RNAi assays demonstrate that ISARL-mediated phospholipid metabolism by phosphatidylserine synthase I is associated with B. burgdorferi survival.
evidence: RNA-seq data showed PTDSS1 is downregulated when ISARL is silenced, and RNAi silencing of PTDSS1 reduced B. burgdorferi burden (Figure 2H).

claim: The tick complement C1q-like protein 3 interacts with ISARL.
source: Furthermore, the tick complement C1q-like protein 3 interacts with ISARL, and B. burgdorferi facilitates this process.
evidence: Multiple binding assays (pull-down, co-immunolocalization) demonstrated interaction between C1QL3 and ISARL (Figure 4G-J).

claim: B. burgdorferi facilitates the interaction between C1QL3 and ISARL.
source: Furthermore, the tick complement C1q-like protein 3 interacts with ISARL, and B. burgdorferi facilitates this process.
evidence: C1QL3 expression is upregulated by B. burgdorferi infection (Figure 4B), and silencing C1QL3 prevents B. burgdorferi-induced upregulation of ISARL (Figure 4M).

claim: The full-length ISARL mRNA encodes a protein with 384 amino acid residues.
source: The full-length ISARL mRNA encoded a protein with 384 amino acid residues and 71% amino acid sequence similarity to both the human and mouse adiponectin receptor proteins 1 and 2.
evidence: Sequence analysis of the identified ISARL gene (GenBank number: XP_029831073).

claim: ISARL has 71% amino acid sequence similarity to both human and mouse adiponectin receptor proteins 1 and 2.
source: The full-length ISARL mRNA encoded a protein with 384 amino acid residues and 71% amino acid sequence similarity to both the human and mouse adiponectin receptor proteins 1 and 2.
evidence: Sequence alignment and similarity analysis comparing ISARL with human and mouse adiponectin receptors.

claim: ISARL has high similarity (87%) to homologs from insect species, including the D. melanogaster adiponectin receptor.
source: It also has high similarity (87%) to homologs from insect species, including the D. melanogaster adiponectin receptor (GenBank number: NP_732759) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 demonstrates high similarity between ISARL and Drosophila adiponectin receptor.

claim: ISARL has seven transmembrane domains.
source: Structure prediction and hydrophobicity analysis indicated that ISARL has seven TM domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Protein structure prediction and hydrophobicity analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The predicted transmembrane regions of adiponectin receptors are highly conserved between vertebrate and invertebrate species, especially in the TM3 domain.
source: Comparison of the amino acid sequences between vertebrate and invertebrate species revealed that the predicted TM regions are highly conserved, especially in the TM3 domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Multiple sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 demonstrates conservation of TM regions.

claim: A blood meal containing B. burgdorferi resulted in significantly increased expression of ISARL in the nymphal tick guts (p<0.0001).
source: Interestingly, a blood meal containing B. burgdorferi resulted in significantly increased expression of ISARL in the nymphal tick guts (p<0.0001) (Figure 1A).
evidence: qPCR data shown in Figure 1A comparing ISARL expression in ticks fed on uninfected vs. B. burgdorferi-infected mice.

claim: Silencing ISARL had no effect on tick feeding behavior.
source: The engorgement weights of ds ISARL-injected nymphs and control ds GFP-injected nymphs were comparable (p>0.05) (Figure 1C), suggesting that silencing ISARL had no effect on tick feeding behavior.
evidence: Engorgement weight measurements shown in Figure 1C show no significant difference between ISARL-silenced and control ticks.

claim: ISARL is associated with B. burgdorferi colonization in the nymphal tick gut.
source: However, ISARL-silenced nymph guts showed a marked reduction of the B. burgdorferi burden (p<0.001) when compared to that in control ticks (Figure 1D), demonstrating that ISARL is associated with B. burgdorferi colonization in the nymphal tick gut.
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 1D showing reduced B. burgdorferi burden in ISARL-silenced ticks.

claim: Silencing ISARL had no observable effect on B. burgdorferi transmission by I. scapularis nymphs.
source: The results showed that B. burgdorferi burdens in the skin of mice (ear skin distal from the tick bite site) at 7, 14, and 21 days post tick detachment, and in heart and joint tissues 21 days post tick detachment were comparable (p>0.05) in mice fed upon by ds GFP- or by ds ISARL-injected nymphs (Figure 1E and F), suggesting that silencing ISARL had no observable effect on B. burgdorferi transmission by I. scapularis nymphs.
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 1E and F showing comparable B. burgdorferi burdens in mice fed upon by control vs. ISARL-silenced ticks.

claim: 18 genes were significantly differentially expressed in the guts of ds ISARL-injected nymphal ticks compared to control after feeding on uninfected mice.
source: After feeding on uninfected mice, 18 genes were significantly differentially expressed in the guts of ds ISARL-injected nymphal ticks when compared to that in control ds GFP-injected tick guts (Figure 2A; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: RNA-seq analysis comparing transcriptomes of ISARL-silenced vs. control ticks fed on uninfected mice, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 35 genes were differentially expressed in tick guts after feeding on B. burgdorferi-infected mice when ISARL was silenced.
source: while 35 genes were differentially expressed after feeding on B. burgdorferi-infected mice (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: RNA-seq analysis comparing transcriptomes of ISARL-silenced vs. control ticks fed on B. burgdorferi-infected mice, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No common genes except ISARL were observed between ticks feeding on uninfected or B. burgdorferi-infected mice when comparing ISARL-silenced to control ticks.
source: No common genes except ISARL were observed between ticks feeding on uninfected or B. burgdorferi-infected mice (Figure 2D), suggesting that the 34 genes (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 1) were all altered by B. burgdorferi, or the influence of B. burgdorferi on the host blood components, rather than blood meal itself, in the absence of ISARL.
evidence: Venn diagram in Figure 2D showing unique and common differentially expressed genes.

claim: Glutathione metabolism was significantly altered in the absence of ISARL after engorgement of ticks on uninfected mice.
source: In particular, based on Gene Ontology (GO) functional classification and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways analyses, glutathione metabolism, including six gamma glutamyl transpeptidase genes (Supplementary file 1), was significantly altered in the absence of ISARL after engorgement of ticks on uninfected mice.
evidence: GO and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses of RNA-seq data from ISARL-silenced ticks fed on uninfected mice.

claim: Many metabolism-associated genes were significantly downregulated in the absence of ISARL after engorging on B. burgdorferi-infected mice.
source: Similarly, many metabolism-associated genes were significantly downregulated in the absence of ISARL after engorging on B. burgdorferi-infected mice (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: RNA-seq data showing downregulation of metabolism genes in ISARL-silenced ticks fed on B. burgdorferi-infected mice.

claim: The most downregulated genes in ISARL-silenced ticks fed on B. burgdorferi-infected mice were involved in fatty acid, lipid and phospholipid, and purine metabolism pathways.
source: GO functional classification and KEGG pathways also showed that the most downregulated genes were involved in fatty acid (e.g., 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase), lipid and phospholipid (e.g., phosphatidylserine synthase I), and purine (e.g., GMP synthase) metabolism pathways after silencing ISARL (Figure 2E)
evidence: GO and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ISARL functions as a metabolic moderator in ticks.
source: GO functional classification and KEGG pathways also showed that the most downregulated genes were involved in fatty acid (e.g., 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase), lipid and phospholipid (e.g., phosphatidylserine synthase I), and purine (e.g., GMP synthase) metabolism pathways after silencing ISARL (Figure 2E), suggesting that ISARL functions as a metabolic moderator in ticks.
evidence: Multiple metabolism pathways are altered when ISARL is silenced, as shown by GO and KEGG analyses in Figure 2E.

claim: PTDSS1 is positively regulated by ISARL.
source: qPCR validation of PTDSS1 showed that PTDSS1 is positively regulated by ISARL.
evidence: qPCR and western blot data in Figure 2F and G showing reduced PTDSS1 expression when ISARL is silenced.

claim: PTDSS1-silenced nymphs showed a marked reduction in the B. burgdorferi burden in the guts compared to control ticks (p<0.05).
source: We found that PTDSS1-silenced nymphs showed a marked reduction in the B. burgdorferi burden in the guts when compared to that in control ticks (p<0.05) (Figure 2H).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 2H showing reduced B. burgdorferi burden in PTDSS1-silenced ticks.

claim: A blood meal containing B. burgdorferi resulted in significantly increased expression of PTDSS1 in the nymphal tick guts (p<0.05).
source: Furthermore, a blood meal containing B. burgdorferi resulted in significantly increased expression of PTDSS1 in the nymphal tick guts (p<0.05) (Figure 2I)
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 2I comparing PTDSS1 expression in ticks fed on uninfected vs. B. burgdorferi-infected mice.

claim: PTDSS1 has a critical role during B. burgdorferi colonization of the tick gut.
source: Furthermore, a blood meal containing B. burgdorferi resulted in significantly increased expression of PTDSS1 in the nymphal tick guts (p<0.05) (Figure 2I), suggesting that PTDSS1 indeed has a critical role during B. burgdorferi colonization of the tick gut.
evidence: PTDSS1 is upregulated by B. burgdorferi infection and its silencing reduces B. burgdorferi burden.

claim: PTDSS1 uses L-serine as the phosphatidyl acceptor to generate phosphatidylserine (PS).
source: PTDSS1 is involved in phospholipid metabolism and mainly uses L-serine as the phosphatidyl acceptor to generate the anionic lipid phosphatidylserine (PS), which serves as a precursor for phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and phosphatidylcholine (PC) synthesis (Figure 2J; Aktas et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from Aktas et al., 2014 and illustrated in Figure 2J showing the phospholipid pathway.

claim: Phosphatidylserine serves as a precursor for phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and phosphatidylcholine (PC) synthesis.
source: PTDSS1 is involved in phospholipid metabolism and mainly uses L-serine as the phosphatidyl acceptor to generate the anionic lipid phosphatidylserine (PS), which serves as a precursor for phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and phosphatidylcholine (PC) synthesis (Figure 2J; Aktas et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from Aktas et al., 2014 and illustrated in Figure 2J showing the phospholipid pathway.

claim: PC is one of the main phospholipids on the cellular membrane of B. burgdorferi.
source: Importantly, PC is one of the main phospholipids on the cellular membrane of B. burgdorferi (Kerstholt et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Kerstholt et al., 2020.

claim: B. burgdorferi lacks the central phospholipid metabolic enzymes.
source: However, B. burgdorferi lacks the central phospholipid metabolic enzymes.
evidence: Statement based on known characteristics of B. burgdorferi genome and metabolism.

claim: Silencing phosphatidylserine decarboxylase (PSD) resulted in a significantly decreased B. burgdorferi burden in tick guts (p<0.05).
source: Interestingly, we also found a significantly decreased B. burgdorferi burden in ds PSD-injected tick guts (p<0.05), and PSD and PTDSS1 elicit a similar degree of reduced B. burgdorferi levels (Figure 2K).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 2K showing reduced B. burgdorferi burden in PSD-silenced ticks.

claim: PSD and PTDSS1 elicit a similar degree of reduced B. burgdorferi levels.
source: Interestingly, we also found a significantly decreased B. burgdorferi burden in ds PSD-injected tick guts (p<0.05), and PSD and PTDSS1 elicit a similar degree of reduced B. burgdorferi levels (Figure 2K).
evidence: Comparison of B. burgdorferi burden reduction in PSD-silenced vs. PTDSS1-silenced ticks shown in Figure 2K.

claim: ISARL-mediated phospholipid metabolic pathways associated with PTDSS1 have a critical role in B. burgdorferi colonization.
source: Taken together, ISARL-mediated phospholipid metabolic pathways associated with PTDSS1 have a critical role in B. burgdorferi colonization.
evidence: Multiple lines of evidence showing ISARL regulates PTDSS1, both are upregulated by B. burgdorferi, and silencing either reduces B. burgdorferi burden.

claim: Tick glucose-6-phosphatase (G6p) was significantly downregulated in the presence of mammalian adiponectin.
source: The data showed that one classic downstream gene of mammalian adiponectin signaling, tick glucose-6-phosphatase (G6p, ISCW017459), was significantly downregulated in the presence of mammalian adiponectin (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A from ticks injected with recombinant mouse adiponectin vs. GFP control.

claim: In mammals, binding of adiponectin to its receptor suppresses G6p and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (Pck) expression through an AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-dependent mechanism.
source: It has been demonstrated that in mammals the binding of adiponectin to its receptor suppresses G6p and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (Pck) expression through an AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-dependent mechanism, which further inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis (Figure 3B; Kadowaki et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from Kadowaki et al., 2006 and illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: Adiponectin-mediated suppression of G6p and Pck inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in mammals.
source: It has been demonstrated that in mammals the binding of adiponectin to its receptor suppresses G6p and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (Pck) expression through an AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-dependent mechanism, which further inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis (Figure 3B; Kadowaki et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from Kadowaki et al., 2006 and illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: G6pc1, G6pc2, Pck2, and Pck3 were significantly downregulated in the tick gut in the presence of adiponectin.
source: Interestingly, G6pc1, G6pc2, Pck2, and Pck3 were significantly downregulated in the tick gut in the presence of adiponectin (Figure 3C).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 3C from ticks injected with recombinant adiponectin vs. GFP control.

claim: G6pc1 and G6pc2 showed significant downregulation in the presence of adiponectin when ticks fed on wild-type vs. Adipoq-/- mice (p<0.05).
source: We then evaluated the expression of five G6p and Pck genes, and found that G6pc1 and G6pc2 also showed significant downregulation in the presence of adiponectin (p<0.05), while Pck gene expression was not altered (p>0.05) (Figure 3E).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 3E comparing gene expression in ticks fed on WT vs. Adipoq-/- mice.

claim: Pck gene expression was not altered when ticks fed on wild-type vs. Adipoq-/- mice (p>0.05).
source: We then evaluated the expression of five G6p and Pck genes, and found that G6pc1 and G6pc2 also showed significant downregulation in the presence of adiponectin (p<0.05), while Pck gene expression was not altered (p>0.05) (Figure 3E).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 3E comparing gene expression in ticks fed on WT vs. Adipoq-/- mice.

claim: No significant difference of the B. burgdorferi burden in ticks feeding on WT and Adipoq-/- mice was noted (p>0.05).
source: No significant difference of the B. burgdorferi burden in ticks feeding on WT and Adipoq-/- mice was noted (p>0.05) (Figure 3G).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 3G comparing B. burgdorferi burden in ticks fed on WT vs. Adipoq-/- mice.

claim: There was no significant difference in the B. burgdorferi burden between control and G6pc1-silenced ticks (p>0.05).
source: Consistent with the previous observation, there was no significant difference in the B. burgdorferi burden between control and G6pc1-silenced ticks (p>0.05) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing B. burgdorferi burden in G6pc1-silenced vs. control ticks.

claim: G6pc2-silenced ticks did not show altered B. burgdorferi levels (p>0.05).
source: G6pc2-silenced ticks also did not show altered B. burgdorferi levels (p>0.05) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing B. burgdorferi burden in G6pc2-silenced vs. control ticks.

claim: The expression of G6pc1 and G6pc2 in the nymphs was not influenced by B. burgdorferi infection (p>0.05).
source: Furthermore, the expression of G6pc1 and G6pc2 in the nymphs was not influenced by B. burgdorferi infection (p>0.05) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 comparing G6pc1 and G6pc2 expression in ticks fed on uninfected vs. B. burgdorferi-infected mice.

claim: G6pc1- or G6pc2-mediated changes do not affect B. burgdorferi colonization of the tick gut.
source: Furthermore, the expression of G6pc1 and G6pc2 in the nymphs was not influenced by B. burgdorferi infection (p>0.05) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that G6pc1- or G6pc2-mediated changes do not affect B. burgdorferi colonization of the tick gut.
evidence: G6pc1 and G6pc2 are not upregulated by B. burgdorferi and their silencing does not affect B. burgdorferi burden.

claim: B. burgdorferi does not influence the adiponectin concentration in murine blood.
source: We found that B. burgdorferi does not influence the adiponectin concentration in murine blood (Figure 3H).
evidence: ELISA data in Figure 3H showing adiponectin concentration in mice sera after B. burgdorferi infection.

claim: Mammalian adiponectin can regulate ISARL-mediated glucose metabolism pathway.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that mammalian adiponectin can regulate ISARL-mediated glucose metabolism pathway; however, it has no effect on B. burgdorferi colonization.
evidence: Adiponectin downregulates G6pc1 and G6pc2 in ticks, demonstrating regulation of glucose metabolism pathway.

claim: Mammalian adiponectin has no effect on B. burgdorferi colonization.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that mammalian adiponectin can regulate ISARL-mediated glucose metabolism pathway; however, it has no effect on B. burgdorferi colonization.
evidence: No difference in B. burgdorferi burden in ticks fed on WT vs. Adipoq-/- mice, and silencing G6pc1/G6pc2 does not affect B. burgdorferi.

claim: Two tick proteins had blastp hits with the human adiponectin C1Q domain.
source: To this end, we performed a blastp search of the I. scapularis genome with the globular C1Q domain of human and mouse adiponectin, which is known to stimulate the adiponectin receptor (Yamauchi et al., 2002). Two tick proteins had blastp hits with the human adiponectin C1Q domain (Figure 4A)
evidence: Blastp search results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The two tick proteins with C1Q domain homology were annotated as complement C1q-like protein 3 (C1QL3) and conserved hypothetical protein.
source: Two tick proteins had blastp hits with the human adiponectin C1Q domain (Figure 4A) and were annotated as complement C1q-like protein 3 (C1QL3) (GenBank number: XP_002415101) and conserved hypothetical protein (GenBank number: EEC18766), respectively.
evidence: Blastp search results and annotation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: C1QL3 and the conserved hypothetical protein are identical proteins except that C1QL3 has a signal peptide sequence.
source: These are identical proteins except that C1QL3 has a signal peptide sequence, and we therefore focused on C1QL3.
evidence: Sequence comparison of the two identified proteins.

claim: A blood meal containing B. burgdorferi resulted in significantly increased expression of C1QL3 in the nymphal tick guts (p<0.01).
source: A blood meal containing B. burgdorferi resulted in significantly increased expression of C1QL3 in the nymphal tick guts (p<0.01) (Figure 4B).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 4B comparing C1QL3 expression in ticks fed on uninfected vs. B. burgdorferi-infected mice.

claim: C1QL3-silenced nymphs had a marked reduction of the B. burgdorferi burden in the guts compared to control ticks (p<0.05).
source: We then generated C1QL3-silenced nymphs and found that these ticks had a marked reduction of the B. burgdorferi burden in the guts when compared to that in control I. scapularis (p<0.05) (Figure 4C).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 4C showing reduced B. burgdorferi burden in C1QL3-silenced ticks.

claim: B. burgdorferi activates the ISARL signaling pathway through the tick C1QL3 protein.
source: This is the same observation as with silencing of ISARL, suggesting that B. burgdorferi activates the ISARL signaling pathway through the tick C1QL3 protein.
evidence: Both ISARL and C1QL3 silencing reduce B. burgdorferi burden, and C1QL3 interacts with ISARL.

claim: Tick C1QL3 C1Q domain has high similarity (64.0%) with the human adiponectin C1Q domain.
source: Because C1QL3 C1Q domain has high similarity (64.0%) with the human adiponectin C1Q domain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Sequence alignment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: C1Q proteins have been demonstrated to activate diverse pathways through the adiponectin receptor.
source: and C1Q proteins have been demonstrated to activate diverse pathways through the adiponectin receptor (Zheng et al., 2011)
evidence: Cited from Zheng et al., 2011.

claim: Tick ISARL can be successfully expressed on the HEK293T cell membrane.
source: The results showed that tick ISARL can be successfully expressed, as validated by cell staining and western blot (Figure 4D and E), on the HEK293T cell membrane (Figure 4D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and western blot data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Recombinant C1QL3 could be detected on the surface of ISARL-expressed rather than empty plasmid-transfected HEK293T cells.
source: After washing and staining, recombinant C1QL3 could be detected on the surface of ISARL-expressed rather than empty plasmid-transfected HEK293T cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data in Figure 4G showing C1QL3 binding to ISARL-expressing cells.

claim: Recombinant C1QL3 interacts with ISARL as demonstrated by pull-down assay.
source: A pull-down assay also indicated that recombinant C1QL3 interacts with ISARL as demonstrated by the detection of C1QL3 only in ISARL-expressed cells pellet (Figure 4H).
evidence: Pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: C1QL3 protein specifically binds to the ISARL-expressed cell membrane.
source: In addition, co-immunolocalization demonstrated that the C1QL3 protein specifically binds to the ISARL-expressed cell membrane (Figure 4I).
evidence: Co-immunolocalization data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: C1QL3 bound to tick ISE6 cells.
source: Furthermore, C1QL3 also bound to tick ISE6 cells, a non-heterologous system (Figure 4J).
evidence: Pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4J demonstrating C1QL3 binding to tick ISE6 cells.

claim: The ISARL transcript level following RNAi silencing of C1QL3 was significantly lower than that in control tick guts after feeding on B. burgdorferi-infected mice (p<0.05).
source: qPCR assessment showed that the ISARL transcript level following RNAi silencing of C1QL3 was significantly lower than that in control ds GFP-injected tick guts after feeding on B. burgdorferi-infected mice (p<0.05) (Figure 4L).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 4L comparing ISARL expression in C1QL3-silenced vs. control ticks.

claim: After silencing C1QL3, a blood meal containing B. burgdorferi did not significantly increase expression of ISARL in the nymphal tick guts compared to feeding on clean mice (p>0.05).
source: More importantly, after silencing C1QL3, a blood meal containing B. burgdorferi did not significantly increase expression of ISARL and PTDSS1 in the nymphal tick guts as compared to feeding on clean mice (p>0.05) (Figure 4M and N)
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 4M comparing ISARL expression in C1QL3-silenced ticks fed on uninfected vs. B. burgdorferi-infected mice.

claim: After silencing C1QL3, a blood meal containing B. burgdorferi did not significantly increase expression of PTDSS1 in the nymphal tick guts compared to feeding on clean mice (p>0.05).
source: More importantly, after silencing C1QL3, a blood meal containing B. burgdorferi did not significantly increase expression of ISARL and PTDSS1 in the nymphal tick guts as compared to feeding on clean mice (p>0.05) (Figure 4M and N)
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 4N comparing PTDSS1 expression in C1QL3-silenced ticks fed on uninfected vs. B. burgdorferi-infected mice.

claim: C1QL3 plays a role in the ISARL signaling and phospholipid metabolism pathways.
source: More importantly, after silencing C1QL3, a blood meal containing B. burgdorferi did not significantly increase expression of ISARL and PTDSS1 in the nymphal tick guts as compared to feeding on clean mice (p>0.05) (Figure 4M and N), further suggesting that C1QL3 plays a role in the ISARL signaling and phospholipid metabolism pathways.
evidence: Silencing C1QL3 prevents B. burgdorferi-induced upregulation of ISARL and PTDSS1.

claim: Adiponectin is a hormone secreted mainly from adipocytes that stimulates glucose utilization and fatty acid oxidation.
source: Adiponectin is a hormone, secreted mainly from adipocytes, that stimulates glucose utilization and fatty acid oxidation (Berg et al., 2001; Fruebis et al., 2001).
evidence: Cited from Berg et al., 2001 and Fruebis et al., 2001.

claim: The key roles of adiponectin in regulating energy homeostasis are mediated by adiponectin receptors across species including humans, yeast, nematodes, and flies.
source: The key roles of adiponectin in regulating energy homeostasis are mediated by adiponectin receptors across species including humans, yeast, nematodes, and flies (Kwak et al., 2013; Narasimhan et al., 2005; Svensson et al., 2011; Yamauchi et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from Kwak et al., 2013; Narasimhan et al., 2005; Svensson et al., 2011; Yamauchi et al., 2003.

claim: ISARL contains the canonical features of adiponectin receptors, including conserved TM domains, a long internal N-terminal region, and a relatively short external C-terminal region.
source: In addition, ISARL contains the canonical features of adiponectin receptors, including conserved TM domains, a long internal N-terminal region, and a relatively short external C-terminal region.
evidence: Structural analysis and comparison with known adiponectin receptors.

claim: Homologs of adiponectin have not yet been identified in arthropods.
source: However, homologs of adiponectin have not yet been identified in arthropods, suggesting that ligands for adiponectin receptors in arthropods may interact in different ways than in vertebrates.
evidence: Database searches did not identify adiponectin homologs in arthropod genomes.

claim: Ligands for adiponectin receptors in arthropods may interact in different ways than in vertebrates.
source: However, homologs of adiponectin have not yet been identified in arthropods, suggesting that ligands for adiponectin receptors in arthropods may interact in different ways than in vertebrates.
evidence: Absence of adiponectin in arthropods despite presence of adiponectin receptors suggests alternative activation mechanisms.

claim: B. burgdorferi engages in intimate interactions with I. scapularis during its acquisition and colonization of the tick gut.
source: The Lyme disease agent, B. burgdorferi, engages in intimate interactions with I. scapularis during its acquisition and colonization of the tick gut (Radolf et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from Radolf et al., 2012.

claim: B. burgdorferi colonization is accompanied by dramatic changes in the expression profiles of Borrelia and tick gut genes.
source: This is accompanied by dramatic changes in the expression profiles of Borrelia and tick gut genes, which are critical drivers for colonization, persistence, or transmission (Kurokawa et al., 2020; Narasimhan et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Kurokawa et al., 2020 and Narasimhan et al., 2017.

claim: The upregulation of ISARL correlates with Borrelia infection in the gut.
source: In our study, expression of ISARL was significantly increased in the nymphal tick gut after B. burgdorferi infection. The upregulation of ISARL correlates with Borrelia infection in the gut.
evidence: ISARL expression is significantly increased after B. burgdorferi infection as shown by qPCR data.

claim: ISARL facilitates B. burgdorferi colonization.
source: More interestingly, after silencing ISARL expression in the tick gut by anal pore injection, nymphal tick guts showed a marked reduction in the B. burgdorferi burden when compared to that in control ticks, demonstrating that ISARL facilitates B. burgdorferi colonization.
evidence: Silencing ISARL reduces B. burgdorferi burden in tick guts.

claim: ISARL can regulate a critical enzyme involved in phospholipid metabolism, PTDSS1.
source: Of note, ISARL can regulate a critical enzyme involved in phospholipid metabolism, PTDSS1.
evidence: RNA-seq and qPCR data show PTDSS1 is downregulated when ISARL is silenced.

claim: Regulation of PTDSS1 by adiponectin receptors is found in yeast.
source: Regulation of PTDSS1 by adiponectin receptors is also found in other organisms such as yeast, where the adiponectin receptor homolog Izh2 is connected to phospholipid metabolism through co-regulation of the expression of inositol-3-phosphate synthase (INO1) and phosphatidylserine synthase (CHO1, homolog of PTDSS1) genes with zinc-responsive activator protein (Zap1) (Mattiazzi Ušaj et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Mattiazzi Ušaj et al., 2015.

claim: Silencing of I. scapularis PTDSS1 led to a reduced spirochete burden in the guts.
source: Silencing of I. scapularis PTDSS1 led to a reduced spirochete burden in the guts, thereby linking B. burgdorferi colonization with phospholipid metabolism.
evidence: qPCR data showing reduced B. burgdorferi burden in PTDSS1-silenced ticks.

claim: B. burgdorferi colonization is linked with phospholipid metabolism.
source: Silencing of I. scapularis PTDSS1 led to a reduced spirochete burden in the guts, thereby linking B. burgdorferi colonization with phospholipid metabolism.
evidence: PTDSS1 is involved in phospholipid metabolism and its silencing reduces B. burgdorferi burden.

claim: The B. burgdorferi genome is small and encodes a limited number of metabolic enzymes.
source: The B. burgdorferi genome is small and encodes a limited number of metabolic enzymes (Casjens et al., 2000; Fraser et al., 1997).
evidence: Cited from Casjens et al., 2000 and Fraser et al., 1997.

claim: The restricted biosynthetic capability forces B. burgdorferi to rely on its vertebrate and arthropod hosts for nutrients or enzymes that it cannot synthesize.
source: The restricted biosynthetic capability forces B. burgdorferi to rely on its vertebrate and arthropod hosts for nutrients or enzymes that it cannot synthesize (Tilly et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from Tilly et al., 2008.

claim: Silencing of I. scapularis 3HADH decreased the B. burgdorferi burden in tick gut.
source: Interestingly, we also found that silencing of I. scapularis 3HADH, which is involved in fatty acid metabolic processes, decreased the B. burgdorferi burden in tick gut (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 showing reduced B. burgdorferi burden in 3HADH-silenced ticks.

claim: The spirochete may require the tick for selected metabolic needs.
source: The markedly decreased B. burgdorferi burden in ticks after silencing of PTDSS1, PSD, and 3HADH suggests that the spirochete may require the tick for selected metabolic needs.
evidence: Multiple metabolic enzymes when silenced reduce B. burgdorferi burden, suggesting metabolic dependence.

claim: Feeding ticks provide Lyme disease spirochetes with glycerol, an alternative carbohydrate energy source and essential building block for phospholipid biosynthesis.
source: Indeed, previous studies have demonstrated that feeding ticks provide Lyme disease spirochetes with glycerol, an alternative carbohydrate energy source and essential building block for phospholipid biosynthesis (Kerstholt et al., 2020; Pappas et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from Kerstholt et al., 2020 and Pappas et al., 2011.

claim: B. burgdorferi can acquire lipids from the membranes of eukaryotic cells to which they are attached.
source: In addition, B. burgdorferi can also acquire lipids from the membranes of eukaryotic cells to which they are attached (Crowley et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Crowley et al., 2013.

claim: B. burgdorferi can upregulate an adiponectin-related protein, C1QL3, in ticks.
source: We also found that B. burgdorferi can upregulate an adiponectin-related protein, C1QL3, in ticks, which associates with ISARL and leads to phospholipid metabolism changes in ticks.
evidence: qPCR data showing C1QL3 is upregulated by B. burgdorferi infection.

claim: C1QL3 associates with ISARL and leads to phospholipid metabolism changes in ticks.
source: We also found that B. burgdorferi can upregulate an adiponectin-related protein, C1QL3, in ticks, which associates with ISARL and leads to phospholipid metabolism changes in ticks.
evidence: C1QL3 binds to ISARL, and silencing C1QL3 prevents B. burgdorferi-induced upregulation of ISARL and PTDSS1.

claim: C1QL3 in tick is mainly involved in metabolism, rather than complement activation.
source: We propose that C1QL3 in tick is mainly involved in metabolism, rather than complement activation, as demonstrated by the decreased B. burgdorferi level after silencing C1QL3.
evidence: Silencing C1QL3 reduces B. burgdorferi burden, suggesting a role in metabolism that supports B. burgdorferi rather than immune defense.

claim: Some C1Q/TNF family proteins are associated with metabolism.
source: Indeed, some of C1Q/TNF family proteins are associated with metabolism.
evidence: General knowledge about C1Q/TNF family proteins.

claim: Proteins such as C1Q/TNF-related protein 3 (CTRP3), CTRP5, CTRP9, CTRP13 (C1QL3), and CTRP15 belong to adipokine family and have been reported to be associated with the regulation of glucose, lipid, or other metabolisms.
source: In addition to adiponectin, proteins such as C1Q/TNF-related protein 3 (CTRP3), CTRP5, CTRP9, CTRP13 (C1QL3), and CTRP15 also belong to adipokine family and have been reported to be associated with the regulation of glucose, lipid, or other metabolisms (Jiang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2017; Mi et al., 2019; Wei et al., 2011; Wolf et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from Jiang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2017; Mi et al., 2019; Wei et al., 2011; Wolf et al., 2016.

claim: AdipoR1 and AdipoR2 double-knockout mice have increased triglyceride levels and exhibit insulin resistance.
source: Interestingly, AdipoR1 and AdipoR2 double-knockout mice have increased triglyceride levels and exhibit insulin resistance, demonstrating that AdipoR1 and AdipoR2 regulate lipid and glucose homeostasis (Kadowaki et al., 2006; Yamauchi et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from Kadowaki et al., 2006 and Yamauchi et al., 2007.

claim: AdipoR1 and AdipoR2 regulate lipid and glucose homeostasis.
source: Interestingly, AdipoR1 and AdipoR2 double-knockout mice have increased triglyceride levels and exhibit insulin resistance, demonstrating that AdipoR1 and AdipoR2 regulate lipid and glucose homeostasis (Kadowaki et al., 2006; Yamauchi et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from Kadowaki et al., 2006 and Yamauchi et al., 2007.

claim: In yeast, a homolog of mammalian adiponectin receptors, ORE20/PHO36, is involved in lipid and phosphate metabolism.
source: In yeast, a homolog of mammalian adiponectin receptors, ORE20/PHO36, is involved in lipid and phosphate metabolism (Karpichev et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from Karpichev et al., 2002.

claim: PHO36 can interact with a plant protein, osmotin, a homolog of mammalian adiponectin, thereby controlling apoptosis in yeast.
source: PHO36 can also interact with a plant protein, osmotin, a homolog of mammalian adiponectin, thereby controlling apoptosis in yeast (Narasimhan et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited from Narasimhan et al., 2005.

claim: An adiponectin receptor that regulates insulin secretion and controls glucose and lipid metabolism was characterized in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: By utilizing the amino acid sequence homology search in other model arthropods, adiponectin was not identified from Drosophila melanogaster; however, an adiponectin receptor that regulates insulin secretion and controls glucose and lipid metabolism was characterized (Kwak et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Kwak et al., 2013.

claim: Infection with B. mori nucleopolyhedrovirus significantly increased adiponectin receptor mRNA levels in the midgut of susceptible B. mori.
source: In addition, Zhu et al., 2008 cloned an adiponectin-like receptor gene from the silk moth, Bombyx mori, and found that infection with B. mori nucleopolyhedrovirus significantly increased adiponectin receptor mRNA levels in the midgut of susceptible B. mori, suggesting an association with pathogen infectivity.
evidence: Cited from Zhu et al., 2008.

claim: B. burgdorferi causes approximately 300,000 cases of Lyme disease annually in the United States.
source: Ixodes scapularis, the black-legged tick, is an important vector of the Lyme disease agent, Borrelia burgdorferi (Estrada-Peña and Jongejan, 1999), which causes approximately 300,000 cases annually in the United States (Rosenberg et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Rosenberg et al., 2018.

claim: B. burgdorferi is acquired when larval or nymphal ticks feed on infected animals, and is transmitted by nymphs or adults to vertebrate hosts.
source: B. burgdorferi is acquired when larval or nymphal ticks feed on infected animals, and is transmitted by nymphs or adults to vertebrate hosts (Kurokawa et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Kurokawa et al., 2020.

claim: Lyme disease in humans manifests as a multisystem disorder of the skin and other organs.
source: Lyme disease in humans manifests as a multisystem disorder of the skin and other organs (e.g., joints, heart, and nervous system), resulting in patients experiencing cardiac, neurological, and arthritic complications (Asch et al., 1994; Singh and Girschick, 2004).
evidence: Cited from Asch et al., 1994 and Singh and Girschick, 2004.

claim: A human vaccine against Lyme disease was approved by the FDA but is not currently available.
source: A human vaccine against Lyme disease was approved by the FDA but is not currently available (Steere et al., 1998).
evidence: Cited from Steere et al., 1998.

claim: Targeting tick proteins has the potential to disrupt tick feeding and alter B. burgdorferi colonization or transmission.
source: Targeting tick proteins has the potential to disrupt tick feeding and alter B. burgdorferi colonization or transmission (Kurokawa et al., 2020), thereby offering a new way to interfere with the life cycle of the Lyme disease spirochete.
evidence: Cited from Kurokawa et al., 2020.

claim: An I. scapularis adiponectin receptor-like (ISARL) protein facilitates B. burgdorferi colonization of the tick.
source: In the present study, we demonstrate that an I. scapularis adiponectin receptor-like (ISARL) protein facilitates B. burgdorferi colonization of the tick.
evidence: ISARL is upregulated by B. burgdorferi infection and its silencing reduces B. burgdorferi burden.

claim: ISARL-mediated stimulation of I. scapularis metabolic pathways are associated with spirochete colonization.
source: ISARL-mediated stimulation of I. scapularis metabolic pathways are associated with spirochete colonization, and a tick complement C1q-like protein 3 contributes to ISARL activation.
evidence: RNA-seq shows ISARL regulates metabolic pathways, and silencing ISARL or these pathways reduces B. burgdorferi burden.

claim: A tick complement C1q-like protein 3 contributes to ISARL activation.
source: ISARL-mediated stimulation of I. scapularis metabolic pathways are associated with spirochete colonization, and a tick complement C1q-like protein 3 contributes to ISARL activation.
evidence: C1QL3 binds to ISARL, and silencing C1QL3 prevents B. burgdorferi-induced upregulation of ISARL.

claim: This study identifies a new tick metabolic pathway that is connected to the life cycle of the Lyme disease spirochete.
source: This study identifies a new tick metabolic pathway that is connected to the life cycle of the Lyme disease spirochete.
evidence: The study demonstrates ISARL-mediated phospholipid metabolism is important for B. burgdorferi colonization.

claim: Adiponectin mediates its actions mainly via binding adiponectin receptors with its globular C1q domain.
source: Adiponectin mediates its actions mainly via binding adiponectin receptors with its globular C1q domain (Buechler et al., 2010; Yamauchi et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from Buechler et al., 2010 and Yamauchi et al., 2002.

claim: Two adiponectin receptors, AdipoR1 and AdipoR2, have been identified in mammals.
source: Two adiponectin receptors, AdipoR1 and AdipoR2, have been identified in mammals (Yamauchi et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from Yamauchi et al., 2003.

claim: AdipoR1 and R2 belong to a family of membrane receptors predicted to contain seven transmembrane (TM) domains with an internal N terminus and an external C terminus.
source: AdipoR1 and R2 belong to a family of membrane receptors predicted to contain seven transmembrane (TM) domains with an internal N terminus and an external C terminus (Yamauchi et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from Yamauchi et al., 2003.

claim: AdipoR1 has a higher binding affinity for the globular form of adiponectin.
source: AdipoR1 has a higher binding affinity for the globular form of adiponectin, whereas AdipoR2 has a greater affinity for full-length adiponectin (Yamauchi et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from Yamauchi et al., 2003.

claim: AdipoR2 has a greater affinity for full-length adiponectin.
source: AdipoR1 has a higher binding affinity for the globular form of adiponectin, whereas AdipoR2 has a greater affinity for full-length adiponectin (Yamauchi et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from Yamauchi et al., 2003.

claim: Mutant of the AdipoR1 gene in retinal pigment epithelial cells results in the inability to take up and retain docosahexaenoic acid (DHA).
source: For instance, mutant of the AdipoR1 gene in retinal pigment epithelial cells results in the inability to take up and retain the essential fatty acid family member docosahexaenoic acid (DHA, 22:6,n-3), further leading to photoreceptor cell death and retinal degeneration (Rice et al., 2015; Sluch et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Rice et al., 2015 and Sluch et al., 2018.

claim: Mutant of the AdipoR1 gene in retinal pigment epithelial cells leads to photoreceptor cell death and retinal degeneration.
source: For instance, mutant of the AdipoR1 gene in retinal pigment epithelial cells results in the inability to take up and retain the essential fatty acid family member docosahexaenoic acid (DHA, 22:6,n-3), further leading to photoreceptor cell death and retinal degeneration (Rice et al., 2015; Sluch et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Rice et al., 2015 and Sluch et al., 2018.

claim: Adiponectin receptors are thought to have ceramidase activity.
source: Adiponectin receptors are thought to have ceramidase activity (Vasiliauskaité-Brooks et al., 2017), which is critical for cell survival through formation of antiapoptotic metabolite-sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) (Holland et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from Vasiliauskaité-Brooks et al., 2017.

claim: Ceramidase activity is critical for cell survival through formation of antiapoptotic metabolite-sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P).
source: Adiponectin receptors are thought to have ceramidase activity (Vasiliauskaité-Brooks et al., 2017), which is critical for cell survival through formation of antiapoptotic metabolite-sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) (Holland et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from Holland et al., 2011.

claim: ISARL plays a key role in metabolic pathways in I. scapularis.
source: In summary, we demonstrate that ISARL plays a key role in metabolic pathways in I. scapularis.
evidence: RNA-seq data shows multiple metabolic pathways are altered when ISARL is silenced.

claim: ISARL-mediated phospholipid metabolism by PTDSS1 contributes to B. burgdorferi colonization.
source: ISARL-mediated phospholipid metabolism by PTDSS1 contributes to B. burgdorferi colonization and an adiponectin-related protein, C1QL3, is involved in ISARL signaling pathway.
evidence: ISARL regulates PTDSS1, and silencing either reduces B. burgdorferi burden.

claim: An adiponectin-related protein, C1QL3, is involved in ISARL signaling pathway.
source: ISARL-mediated phospholipid metabolism by PTDSS1 contributes to B. burgdorferi colonization and an adiponectin-related protein, C1QL3, is involved in ISARL signaling pathway.
evidence: C1QL3 binds to ISARL and silencing C1QL3 prevents B. burgdorferi-induced upregulation of ISARL and PTDSS1.

claim: B. burgdorferi co-opts the activation of the ISARL pathway to facilitate colonization of I. scapularis.
source: These studies elucidate a new pathway involved in tick metabolism and demonstrate that B. burgdorferi co-opts the activation of this pathway to facilitate colonization of I. scapularis.
evidence: B. burgdorferi infection upregulates ISARL and C1QL3, which activate metabolic pathways that support B. burgdorferi colonization.

claim: These processes are crucial to understanding the complex life cycle of the Lyme disease agent within ticks.
source: These processes are crucial to understanding the complex life cycle of the Lyme disease agent within ticks, and may be applicable to other arthropods and arthropod-borne infectious agents.
evidence: The study reveals how B. burgdorferi manipulates tick metabolism for colonization.

claim: These findings may be applicable to other arthropods and arthropod-borne infectious agents.
source: These processes are crucial to understanding the complex life cycle of the Lyme disease agent within ticks, and may be applicable to other arthropods and arthropod-borne infectious agents.
evidence: The mechanisms identified may be conserved across arthropod vectors.
